transcript.content: Hello. What brings you in to see me today?
I’ve been having a really hard time lately because I feel like I can't properly listen when people are talking directly to me. It's like my mind just drifts off even when I
Is this difficulty paying attention a relatively recent change for you, or is it something you've struggled with for as long as you can remember, even back in childhood?

It's definitely not a new thing, as I've struggled with these attention issues since I was a kid, well before I turned 12. However, it has become a really constant and prominent struggle for about the last year and five months.
Along with these attention struggles, did you also tend to fidget, feel physically restless, or have a hard time staying still, especially when you were younger?

Yes, absolutely. I've always fidgeted a lot, like constantly tapping my feet and squirming, and I really struggle to stay seated when I'm expected to. This physical restlessness has been a constant thing for me ever since I was a young kid, well before age 12.

latest_inference.note: Previously, the candidates included both Inattentive and Combined presentations of ADHD, as well as Major Depressive Disorder and Generalized Anxiety Disorder. In this turn, the patient confirmed significant, persistent symptoms of both inattention (difficulty listening, mind drifting) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (fidgeting, foot tapping, difficulty staying seated) starting well before age 12. This rules out the purely Predominantly Inattentive Presentation. There is no current evidence supporting Major Depressive Disorder or Generalized Anxiety Disorder as primary drivers of these lifelong symptoms, narrowing the diagnosis to Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Combined Presentation).

inference_history.note: This is the initial turn of the interview. The patient's chief complaint of difficulty listening and their mind drifting off during conversations strongly suggests inattention. Therefore, ADHD (Predominantly Inattentive and Combined Presentations) are primary candidates. Cognitive symptoms like poor concentration can also be secondary to Major Depressive Disorder or Generalized Anxiety Disorder, which are included in the initial differential.
